title: Kulko v. Superior Court (1978)
summary: A New York father’s acquiescence in his children’s living with their mother in California did not establish the necessary forum affiliation for the support proceeding.
notes:
Read alongside McGee and Burger King to see why the kind of relationship and the defendant’s own conduct matter. The note does not support a categorical rule that every noncommercial relationship defeats jurisdiction.

The decision was 6-3: Justice Marshall wrote for the Court and Justice Brennan dissented, joined by Justices White and Powell, concluding the father's California connection was not too attenuated to require him to defend there. The Kulkos had married in California during Ezra's military stopover, lived in New York for 13 years, and signed a separation agreement in New York giving the children to the mother in California for summers and holidays.

sections.Parties: The mother sought relief in California concerning support. The father, based in New York, challenged California’s jurisdiction over him.
sections.Material Facts: The parents’ relationship and earlier arrangements were centered outside California. The father allowed the children to live with their mother in California and facilitated their travel. The alleged contact consisted principally of this family decision, rather than the father’s conducting business, seeking commercial advantages, or otherwise undertaking the relevant activity in California.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court rejected California’s assertion of jurisdiction. The casebook presents this result and its rationale as a note rather than reproducing the full opinion.
sections.Issue: Did consenting to the children’s residence in California amount to purposeful availment sufficient to adjudicate support obligations there?
sections.Holding: No. The family accommodation did not supply the needed defendant-created forum relationship.
sections.Reasoning: The Court distinguished a parent’s accommodation of family circumstances from conduct invoking the benefits and protections of the forum in the manner needed to justify the suit. Foreseeable effects on family members within a state did not alone establish jurisdiction. California’s legitimate interest in resident children remained relevant, but it could not replace the absent connection attributable to the father.

learning.why: A New York father’s acquiescence in his children’s living with their mother in California did not establish the necessary forum affiliation for the support proceeding.

topics.purposeful-availment: A parent’s agreement that children could live in California did not constitute purposeful commercial or other forum activity supporting this support claim.
topics.fairness: The state’s interest in children residing there did not itself authorize jurisdiction over their out-of-state parent.
topics.cp-effects-test: The Court rejected treating the financial benefit to the father from the children's California residence as an in-state 'effect' supporting jurisdiction, limiting effects-based theories in non-commercial settings.
topics.minimum-contacts: The case is a minimum-contacts decision holding that acquiescence in a child's move is not a contact the defendant purposefully created.
